title: A standardized infection prevention bundle for reduction of CSF shunt infections in adult ventriculoperitoneal shunt surgery performed without antibiotic-impregnated catheters
article_subtype: Prospective, single-center, single-surgeon quality improvement study comparing periods before and after protocol implementation
condition_or_topic: Prevention of CSF shunt infections after ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt insertion or revision in adults.
clinical_background: Hydrocephalus affects approximately 175 per 100,000 adults and may require permanent CSF diversion with a shunt. Adult shunt surgery can be complicated by device failure and infection; the reported infection risk during the first postoperative year is 5%–15%. Infections can cause substantial morbidity and mortality and commonly require further surgery, prolonged intravenous antibiotics, and longer hospitalization. Protocol-based infection prevention has reduced shunt infections in pediatric QI studies, but evidence on comprehensive protocols for adults is limited.
objectives: Develop a standardized infection prevention bundle using QI methodology and assess whether its implementation reduces infections after adult VP shunt insertion or revision without antibiotic-impregnated catheters.
clinical_question: In adults undergoing VP shunt insertion or revision, does implementation of the Calgary Adult Shunt Infection Prevention Protocol (CASIPP), initially and after a change to preoperative chlorhexidine/alcohol skin antisepsis, compared with surgery without a standardized protocol, reduce shunt-related surgical site infections within 1 year of surgery?
study_design: Prospective, single-center, single-surgeon quality-improvement cohort study comparing shunt infection rates before and after implementation and subsequent modification of a standardized prevention protocol. The study was not randomized. Procedures took place at the Foothills Medical Center between January 2012 and January 2021.

population.description: Adults undergoing VP shunt insertion or revision by one surgeon. The study included 400 patients who underwent 621 procedures.
inclusion_criteria: VP shunt placement or revision by the study surgeon.
exclusion_criteria: Shunt procedures performed by other neurosurgeons.
CSF diversion procedures other than VP shunting.
population.care_setting: Foothills Medical Center, Calgary, Alberta, Canada

interventions: The Calgary Adult Shunt Infection Prevention Protocol (CASIPP), introduced on July 1, 2013, standardized preoperative optimization, sterile precautions for the operative field and staff, and shunt-system-related practices. Its described elements included prophylactic antibiotics, maintenance of core temperature between 36°C and 37.5°C, iodine-impregnated adhesive drapes, and double gloving.
On July 1, 2015, preoperative skin antisepsis within CASIPP changed from povidone-iodine to 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol.
A preoperative chlorhexidine bathing regimen was added in 2018. The protocol did not use antibiotic-impregnated catheters or intrathecal antibiotics injected into the shunt reservoir.
comparators: Procedures performed without a standardized shunt infection prevention protocol from January 2012 until June 2013.
Procedures performed under the initial CASIPP, before the change to chlorhexidine/alcohol skin antisepsis.

primary: Shunt-related surgical site infection within 1 year of surgery, defined using CNISP criteria. Patients were assessed during clinic visits, emergency room visits, and hospital admissions.

statistical_methods: Infection rates were compared across the no-protocol, initial CASIPP, and CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol periods. Continuous variables were summarized as means ± standard deviations; categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Univariable associations with infection were assessed using Fisher’s exact test or a chi-square test with Yates’ correction, as appropriate. Variables with p < 0.10 in univariable analysis entered multivariable logistic regression. Because infection events were few, odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p values for these models were calculated by exact conditional analysis. Two-sided p values < 0.05 were considered significant. Analyses used SAS version 9.4.
follow_up: At least 1 year after each procedure; the reported follow-up duration was 46.1 ± 28.6 mos.
interpretation: In adults undergoing VP shunt insertion or revision, infection rates fell from 5.8% without a standardized protocol to 4.0% with the initial CASIPP and 0% across 379 consecutive procedures after 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol replaced povidone-iodine for skin antisepsis (p < 0.0001). The CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol was independently associated with lower odds of infection than no protocol (exact OR 0.032, 95% CI 0–0.19, p = 0.0005); the initial CASIPP alone was not associated with a significant reduction (exact OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.17–3.57, p = 0.85). The authors consider chlorhexidine/alcohol likely to have made an important contribution, but cannot separate its effect from that of the full bundle and high adherence. These results were achieved without intrathecal antibiotics or antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: In pediatric patients, the HCRN reported an infection-rate reduction from 8.8% to 5.7% after introducing an 11-step protocol; CASIPP shares several measures with it. Okamura et al. reported no infections in 52 adult procedures after introducing a protocol that included vancomycin and gentamycin administration, whereas the present study recorded no infections in 379 consecutive procedures with CASIPP and chlorhexidine/alcohol without intrathecal antibiotics. The authors describe evidence on AICs as mixed: a modified HCRN protocol found no significant infection-rate effect in pediatric patients, while the BASICS trial found fewer infections with AICs than with standard catheters (HR 0.38, 97.5% CI 0.18–0.80) in a population combining children and adults. Prior studies cited by the authors support chlorhexidine/alcohol skin antisepsis and surgical prevention bundles, but do not establish the independent effect of chlorhexidine/alcohol within CASIPP. The authors also cite evidence that checklists and perioperative bundles have reduced infections or other complications in different surgical settings.
clinical_implications: A standardized prevention bundle can substantially reduce VP shunt infections in adults without antibiotic-impregnated catheters or antibiotics injected into the shunt reservoir, according to the authors’ findings.
Adding 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol for preoperative skin antisepsis may have contributed substantially to the reduction, although its individual effect remains uncertain.
The authors regard sustained monitoring, protocol adjustments and adherence to a checklist as potentially important to maintaining infection prevention.
practice_implications: The authors consider CASIPP, whose measures they describe as straightforward and not dependent on intrathecal antibiotics or AICs, potentially transferable to other centers.
The authors emphasize continued review of infection rates and protocol adherence when implementing a shunt infection prevention strategy.
limitations: The study involved one center and operations by a single surgeon with particular expertise in shunt insertion.
Because the study was not randomized, unknown confounding could not be controlled.

Other procedural changes during the study, including neuronavigation for proximal catheter insertion and laparoscopic distal catheter placement, were not accounted for and might have affected the results; the authors consider an infection-prevention benefit from those changes unlikely.
For procedures before CASIPP, the authors could not determine which individual preventive measures had been used or how often.

The small number of infections limited precision in estimating protocol effects and the ability to use more complex analyses addressing possible within-patient correlations, although each of the 11 infections occurred in a different patient.

The specific contributions of chlorhexidine/alcohol skin antisepsis and the later preoperative chlorhexidine bath cannot be distinguished from other bundle components or the already low infection rate.
strengths: Prospective data allowed assessment of the timing of protocol changes relative to infection rates.
The series included n = 621 procedures and is described by the authors as the largest reported adult series on shunt infection prevention.
The IPC independently monitored procedures for infection and met regularly with the neurosurgical team to review infection-related issues and adherence.

Selection bias was considered limited because most eligible adult VP shunt procedures at the center were included; the authors describe the population as diverse and representative of adults with hydrocephalus in the region.
CASIPP uses measures the authors describe as clear and simple to carry out.
The protocol does not require intrathecal antibiotics or AICs, supporting what the authors consider feasible and economical use elsewhere.
open_questions: How much of the infection reduction was attributable specifically to 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol rather than the complete bundle and high adherence?
What specific contribution, if any, did the preoperative chlorhexidine bath make after it was introduced when infection rates were already approaching zero?
Will CASIPP retain its observed effectiveness across other centers and surgeons?
future_directions: Conduct larger, multicenter studies to verify the effectiveness of CASIPP.

main_findings.context: The study included 621 procedures in 400 patients from January 2012 to January 2021. Each infection occurred in a different patient.

Shunt infections occurred after implementation of the initial CASIPP.

main_findings.description: No shunt infections occurred after chlorhexidine/alcohol replaced povidone-iodine within CASIPP; infection rates differed significantly across the study periods.
main_findings.context: The CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol period comprised 379 consecutive procedures (61.0%). The reported rates across the no-protocol, initial CASIPP, and CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol periods were 5.8%, 4.0%, and 0%, respectively.

main_findings.description: After adjustment for procedure type, CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol was independently associated with lower odds of shunt infection than no protocol.
main_findings.context: The multivariable model compared CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol against no protocol and adjusted for new shunt insertion versus revision.

main_findings.description: CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol was associated with lower odds of shunt infection than the initial CASIPP.
main_findings.context: The comparison was reported from the multivariable analysis.

main_findings.description: The initial CASIPP was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in shunt infection compared with no protocol.
main_findings.context: The multivariable table reports 0.726; the accompanying text reports the exact OR as 0.73 for the same comparison.

main_findings.description: In the multivariable analysis, shunt revision was associated with lower odds of infection than new shunt insertion.
main_findings.context: The comparison was revision versus new insertion.

main_findings.description: The examined infections yielded identified organisms; some infections involved more than one organism.
main_findings.context: Multiple organisms were identified in 2 patients. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus accounted for 6 (46.1%) identifications, Staphylococcus aureus for 3 (23.1%), Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes for 2 (15.4%), Corynebacterium species for 1 (7.7%), and Histoplasma capsulatum for 1 (7.7%).

subgroup_analyses: Procedure type was significantly associated with shunt infection (p = 0.01): 10 infections followed new insertion and 1 followed revision. In the univariable table, new insertion accounted for 10 (90.9%) procedures with infection and 320 (52.5%) without infection; revision accounted for 1 (9.1%) with infection and 290 (47.5%) without infection.

Age was not significantly associated with shunt infection (p = 0.13). For ages <60, the groups with and without infection contained 3 (27.3%) and 143 (23.4%) procedures, respectively; for 60 to <75, 6 (54.5%) and 197 (32.3%); for 75 to <80, 2 (18.2%) and 110 (18.0%); and for ≥80, 0 (0%) and 160 (26.3%).

Sex was not significantly associated with shunt infection (p > 0.99). Male patients accounted for 7 (63.6%) procedures with infection and 362 (59.3%) without infection; female patients accounted for 4 (36.4%) and 248 (40.7%), respectively.

Hydrocephalus etiology was not significantly associated with shunt infection (p = 0.38). For acquired hydrocephalus, the groups with and without infection contained 1 (9.1%) and 96 (15.7%) procedures, respectively; for congenital hydrocephalus, 3 (27.3%) and 69 (11.3%); for transitional hydrocephalus, 0 (0%) and 47 (7.7%); and for iNPH, 7 (63.6%) and 398 (65.3%).

The univariable protocol comparison was significant (p < 0.0001). The no-protocol period accounted for 4 (36.4%) procedures with infection and 65 (10.7%) without infection; initial CASIPP accounted for 7 (63.6%) and 166 (27.2%); and CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol accounted for 0 (0%) and 379 (62.1%).

Hydrocephalus etiology did not change significantly across the study periods. The proportion of procedures that were revisions was 44% before the bundle, 47% during initial CASIPP, and 47% after chlorhexidine/alcohol was required for antisepsis.

An additional multivariable model that included categorized age and etiology retained CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol as an independent predictor of fewer shunt infections; its effect was not appreciably diminished relative to the reported model. The authors stated that the limited number of infections prevented reliable inclusion of further variables in the principal model.
secondary_results: Compliance with every protocol element was > 98%. Protocol violations had no significant association with infection.
Across the 621 procedures, 330 (53.1%) were new insertions and 291 (46.9%) were revisions. Follow-up duration was 46.1 ± 28.6 mos.
The distribution of hydrocephalus etiologies across procedures was iNPH 405 (65.2%), acquired 97 (15.6%), congenital 72 (11.6%), and transitional 47 (7.6%).

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that a standardized prevention bundle significantly reduced infections after adult VP shunt surgery without antibiotic-impregnated catheters. They suggest that adding 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol may have contributed substantially, and call for larger multicenter studies to verify the protocol’s effectiveness.
narrative_summary:
This prospective, single-center quality-improvement cohort study assessed infection after adult VP shunt insertion or revision performed by one surgeon. It compared surgery without a standardized protocol, surgery after introduction of CASIPP, and surgery after 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol replaced povidone-iodine for preoperative skin antisepsis. Antibiotic-impregnated catheters were not used. The primary outcome was shunt-related surgical site infection under CNISP criteria, assessed for at least 12 months after surgery.

From January 2012 to January 2021, the study included 621 procedures in 400 patients. Infection occurred after 4 of 69 procedures without a protocol, 7 of 173 with initial CASIPP, and 0 of 379 with CASIPP plus chlorhexidine/alcohol. The corresponding infection rates were 5.8%, 4.0%, and 0% (p < 0.0001). After adjustment for procedure type, CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol was associated with lower infection odds than no protocol (exact OR 0.032, 95% CI 0–0.19, p = 0.0005); the initial CASIPP comparison was not significant. Protocol compliance exceeded > 98% for all elements.

The authors consider the bundle potentially transferable to other centers but cannot isolate the effect of chlorhexidine/alcohol from the complete protocol and high adherence. They note the single-center, single-surgeon, nonrandomized design and the small number of infections as limitations, and recommend larger multicenter verification.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVE
document_sections.content: VP shunt insertion and revision are common neurosurgical operations. In adults, shunt infection remains frequent and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. The study aimed to use QI methods to develop a standardized bundle intended to lower shunt infection rates.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: This was a prospective QI study at one center involving one surgeon. Eligible patients were 18 years of age or older and underwent VP shunt insertion or revision. The primary outcome was shunt-related surgical site infection within 1 year, defined using Canadian Nosocomial Infection Surveillance Program criteria. No standardized protocol existed before July 2013. CASIPP began on July 1, 2013, and was revised on July 1, 2015, when 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol replaced povidone-iodine for preoperative skin antisepsis. Adherence was monitored systematically. Antibiotic-impregnated catheters were not used.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The study included 621 consecutive VP shunt insertions and revisions. Infection rates were 5.8% without a standardized protocol, 4.0% after CASIPP began, and 0% across 379 consecutive procedures after chlorhexidine/alcohol was introduced (p < 0.0001). In multivariable logistic regression, CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol was associated with lower odds of shunt infection (OR 0.032, 95% CI 0–0.19, p = 0.0005).

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: The authors concluded that a standardized adult shunt infection prevention bundle substantially and durably reduced infections without antibiotic-impregnated catheters. They considered preoperative antisepsis with 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol a possible important contributor and called for multicenter studies to confirm the protocol’s effectiveness.

document_sections.heading: A standardized infection prevention bundle for reduction of CSF shunt infections in adult ventriculoperitoneal shunt surgery performed without antibiotic-impregnated catheters
document_sections.content: Hydrocephalus affects approximately 175 per 100,000 adults. Impaired clearance of CSF leads to its progressive accumulation and brain injury. The effective treatments described are endoscopic third ventriculostomy, which diverts CSF within the brain, and permanent diversion away from the brain through an implanted shunt. Common shunt types are VP, ventriculoatrial, and lumboperitoneal; VP implantation is widely performed in children and adults. Although CSF shunts effectively treat adult hydrocephalus, system failure often necessitates revision. Initial and later adult shunt operations carry a high infection risk of 5%–15% during the first postoperative year. Infection causes substantial morbidity and mortality and adversely affects patients and families. It generally entails at least further surgery, prolonged intravenous antibiotics, and a longer hospital stay; average direct hospital costs are between $50,000 and $100,000 USD per infection. Numerous perioperative and intraoperative preventive strategies have been proposed. High-quality randomized clinical trials had not been undertaken for shunt infection prevention bundles, but pediatric QI studies had provided convincing evidence that standardized, protocol-based bundles reduce infections. At multiple member sites, the HCRN 11-step protocol was associated with a decline from 8.8% to 5.7% among 1571 pediatric patients. Yang et al. also reported a lower infection rate after introducing that protocol at a nonmember pediatric site. Okamura et al. had published findings on a prevention protocol involving 52 adult patients, but comprehensive adult studies remained lacking. The authors therefore sought to develop and assess a standardized bundle for adults undergoing VP shunt insertion or revision, hypothesizing that infections would decline over time without antibiotic-impregnated CSF shunts.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: This prospective cohort QI initiative compared postoperative shunt infection rates before and after introduction of a standardized protocol at Foothills Medical Center (FMC) in Calgary, Alberta, Canada. One surgeon performed the operations. Reporting followed the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE 2.0) guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Shunt Protocol
document_sections.content: Before this initiative, the institution had no standardized infection reduction protocol for CSF shunt procedures, although preoperative intravenous antibiotics and povidone-iodine skin preparation were usually used. Neurosurgery and Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) personnel met to develop, refine, and implement CASIPP. A literature review, including the successful HCRN protocol, informed its components. Prophylactic antibiotics and maintenance of normothermia were included because earlier studies associated antibiotics administered at least 30 minutes before skin incision and continued normothermia with fewer surgical site infections. Normothermia meant a core temperature between 36°C and 37.5°C, monitored by anesthesia during surgery. Iodine-impregnated adhesive surgical drapes, such as Ioban, were included because evidence from other operations suggested that limiting skin contact with implants and securing the drapes could reduce infection. In Bejko et al.’s study of 5100 cardiovascular surgery patients, an Ioban drape significantly lowered surgical site infection rates (6.5% vs 1.9%, p = 0.001). Double gloving was included on the basis of earlier shunt studies. Tulipan and Cleves observed infection rates of 15.2% with single gloves and 6.7% with double gloves among 863 patients undergoing CSF diversion (p = 0.0002). Kulkarni et al. identified shunt handling after a surgical glove breach as a significant predictor of infection. Evidence of benefit relative to risks and costs in adults was considered insufficient to include either intrathecal antibiotic injection into the reservoir during surgery or AICs. The selected elements covered 1) preoperative optimization, 2) perioperative field sterile precautions, 3) perioperative staff sterile precautions, and 4) shunt-system factors. CASIPP was introduced on July 1, 2013; neurosurgery and IPC teams subsequently met regularly to review infections and potential modifications. On July 1, 2015, 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol replaced povidone-iodine for preoperative antisepsis because studies had found the former superior. A preoperative chlorhexidine bathing regimen was added in 2018 because it was considered low risk and had reduced postoperative infections in certain populations. FIG. 1 depicts the final protocol.

document_sections.heading: Patient Population
document_sections.content: The Calgary Adult Hydrocephalus Clinic Database and IPC records were used to establish a baseline over 18 months, from January 2012 until June 2013, without a standardized protocol. IPC reviewed documented VP shunt operations for positive CSF cultures and assessed the records of identified patients against CNISP criteria. Consecutive patients operated on by one experienced neurosurgeon, M.G.H., at FMC between January 2012 and January 2021 were assessed. Eligibility required age ≥ 18 years and VP shunt placement or revision. Operations occasionally performed by other neurosurgeons were excluded to maintain a uniform population, as were CSF diversion operations other than VP shunting. Minimum postoperative follow-up was 1 year. TABLE 1 sets out the CNISP diagnostic criteria: with a shunt in place, a microbe isolated from CSF had to be accompanied by ≥1 of fever (≥38.0°C), neurological signs or symptoms, abdominal signs or symptoms, or signs or symptoms of shunt malfunction or obstruction.

document_sections.heading: Data Collection and Variables
document_sections.content: Data were gathered prospectively both before and after CASIPP implementation. Infection rates without a standardized protocol were recorded from January 1, 2012, to July 1, 2013; data collection after implementation on July 1, 2013, continued until January 2021. Chart and operative-note review characterized patients and infected shunts. Recorded variables were age, sex, hydrocephalus etiology, and procedure type. Etiology categories were acquired, unrecognized congenital, transitional, and iNPH. An operation counted as insertion when every hardware component was newly placed; it counted as revision when at least one existing component remained afterward. The analysis distinguished the “no protocol,” “initial CASIPP,” and “CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol” periods. After each operation, the senior author used a checklist to record protocol adherence; that checklist is referenced in Supplementary Fig. 1.

document_sections.heading: Outcome Measure
document_sections.content: The primary outcome was a shunt-related surgical site infection meeting CNISP criteria, as outlined in TABLE 1. Potential infections were assessed through clinic visits, emergency department visits, and hospital admissions for at least 12 months after each operation. The secondary outcome was adherence to the CASIPP checklist referenced in Supplementary Fig. 1.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: The main analysis compared infection rates across the no-protocol, initial-CASIPP, and chlorhexidine/alcohol-CASIPP periods. Continuous variables were summarized as means ± standard deviations; categorical variables as frequencies (n) and percentages. Univariable associations between categorized factors and infection were assessed with Fisher’s exact test or the chi-square test with Yates’ correction, as appropriate. Variables with p < 0.10 in univariable analysis entered multivariable logistic regression. Because outcome events were few, model odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p values were calculated by exact conditional analysis. Two-sided p values < 0.05 were deemed significant. Analyses used SAS version 9.4.

document_sections.heading: Ethics
document_sections.content: The University of Calgary Conjoint Health Research Ethics Board assessed the planned QI initiative and considered it exempt from review. After the QI study, approval was obtained for detailed analysis with a consent waiver.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: From January 2012 through January 2021, 400 patients underwent 621 procedures: 69 (11.1%) before a protocol, 173 (27.9%) under initial CASIPP, and 379 (61.0%) after chlorhexidine/alcohol became the preoperative skin preparation. The most frequent hydrocephalus etiology was iNPH (65.2%); acquired, unrecognized congenital, and transitional etiologies accounted for 15.6%, 11.6%, and 7.6%, respectively. New insertions represented 53.1% of procedures; the remainder were revisions. Etiology did not change significantly over time. Revision proportions were similar across periods: 44% before the bundle, 47% with initial CASIPP, and 47% after chlorhexidine/alcohol was required. TABLE 2 presents baseline characteristics and follow-up duration. There were 11 infections: 4 without a protocol, 7 with initial CASIPP, and none after the antisepsis substitution. Corresponding rates were 5.8%, 4.0%, and 0% (p < 0.0001). Ten infections followed new insertion and 1 followed revision; procedure type was significantly associated with infection (p = 0.01). Infection was not significantly associated with age (p = 0.13), sex (p > 0.99), or hydrocephalus etiology (p = 0.38). TABLE 3 displays the univariable patient and procedure comparisons. Across the infections, 13 organisms were identified; coagulase-negative Staphylococcus was most frequent (46.1%), followed by Staphylococcus aureus (23.1%). Multiple organisms were found in 2 patients. TABLE 4 lists the organisms. Relative to no protocol, CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol remained independently associated with lower infection risk after adjustment for new insertion versus revision (exact OR 0.032, 95% CI 0–0.19, p = 0.0005). Relative to initial CASIPP, it was likewise associated with reduced risk (exact OR 0.042, 95% CI 0–0.22, p = 0.0002). Initial CASIPP did not significantly reduce infections relative to no protocol (exact OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.17–3.57, p = 0.85). TABLE 5 gives the multivariable results. Too few infections occurred to include further variables reliably. Other assessed factors were not significantly associated with infection; even in an overadjusted model incorporating categorized age and etiology, CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol remained an independent predictor of fewer infections, with little change in its estimated effect. Adherence exceeded > 98% for every element, and protocol breaches had no significant association with infection.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors interpret the decline from 5.8% without the bundle to 4.0% after initial CASIPP and 0% over 379 consecutive operations after replacing povidone-iodine with chlorhexidine/alcohol as a significant reduction in adult shunt infections. The adjusted analysis identified CASIPP with chlorhexidine/alcohol as an independent predictor of lower infection rates. FIG. 2 depicts rates of 5.8%, 4.0%, and 0.0%, respectively (p < 0.0001), as well as less variation in infection numbers over time. Neither intraoperative intrathecal antibiotics injected into the reservoir nor antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters were part of the protocol.

document_sections.heading: Shunt Infection Prevention Protocols
document_sections.content: The HCRN introduced an 11-step protocol at four pediatric centers and reported a reduction in infection rates from 8.8% to 5.7%. CASIPP shared elements including 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol, double gloving, and Ioban drapes. Okamura et al. examined an adult first-time-shunting protocol using povidone-iodine skin preparation, immersion of the device in a vancomycin solution before insertion, and injection of vancomycin and gentamycin into the reservoir afterward. They observed no infections in 52 procedures after introducing their protocol. The present authors likewise observed no infections with CASIPP plus chlorhexidine/alcohol across 379 consecutive adult procedures, without intrathecal antibiotics.

document_sections.heading: Antibiotic-Impregnated Catheters
document_sections.content: The authors describe continuing disagreement over whether AICs should be mandatory in shunt surgery because reported infection reduction has been inconsistent. In 2016, the HCRN reported that AICs had no significant effect within its modified pediatric protocol. Across eight centers, infection was 6% (95% CI 5.1%–7.2%), not significantly different from 5.7% (95% CI 4.6%–7.0%) under the original protocol; those investigators considered AIC effectiveness uncertain. Potential treatment-related complications have also been proposed. A systematic review by Konstantelias et al. found more shunt infections due to methicillin-resistant S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli with these catheters. The present authors excluded AICs from CASIPP because the literature was inconclusive. The three-arm BASICS randomized trial, published in 2019, enrolled 1605 patients receiving their first VP shunt and assigned standard, AIC, or silver catheters. AIC recipients had significantly fewer infections than standard-catheter recipients (HR 0.38, 97.5% CI 0.18–0.80). Infection declined from 6% to 2% in the AIC group overall, but the trial included children and adults. Regardless of randomized group, infection rates were 7.9% among 592 pediatric patients, 4.6% among 499 adults < 65 years of age, and 1% among 503 adults ≥ 65 years of age. The authors note that adult and older-adult baseline rates were low and that their own rate had reached zero before BASICS appeared; they therefore saw no need to reconsider adding AICs.

document_sections.heading: Chlorhexidine
document_sections.content: Several cited studies found 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol superior to povidone-iodine for preoperative antisepsis. In a randomized trial across six centers, Darouiche et al. reported infection rates of 16.1% with povidone-iodine versus 9.5% with chlorhexidine-alcohol (p = 0.004). Studies of implanted surgical hardware also associated chlorhexidine with fewer postoperative infections. In their systematic review of pediatric CSF shunt infection prevention interventions, Sarmey et al. found chlorhexidine use associated with a significant reduction in postoperative shunt infections. The present study cannot isolate the effect of adding chlorhexidine/alcohol: the outcome may reflect the complete bundle together with the antiseptic change and high adherence. Nonetheless, its data suggest an important role for the antiseptic change. Preoperative chlorhexidine bathing had also reduced postoperative infections elsewhere. In a randomized hip and knee arthroplasty trial by Kapadia et al., one group bathed with chlorhexidine the night before and morning of surgery, while the usual-care group used antibacterial soap; infection odds were significantly higher with usual care (OR 8.15, 95% CI 1.01–65.6, p = 0.049). The authors added bathing to CASIPP in early 2018 because they considered it low risk with potentially substantial benefit. As infection was already uncommon, its specific contribution cannot be determined, although the shunt infection rate stayed at zero for the 3 years after bathing was introduced.

document_sections.heading: Use of Bundles in Other Operative Settings
document_sections.content: The authors emphasize the value of operative protocols and checklists for reducing complications, including surgical site infections. They describe how checklists may change individual and system behavior by increasing staff awareness of infection risks. In an intensive care unit study, Pronovost et al. reported that a standardized checklist lowered central venous catheter infection rates per 1000 catheter days from 2.7 to zero at 3 months (p = 0.002). Haynes et al. designed a surgical checklist based on WHO safe-surgery guidance and prospectively studied 3733 patients before implementation and 3955 afterward at eight hospitals. Deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% (p = 0.003), and inpatient complications from 11% to 7% (p < 0.001). In a randomized trial involving 236 adults undergoing surgery, Loftus et al. found that a perioperative prevention bundle significantly lowered surgical site infection risk relative to usual care (HR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02–0.92, p = 0.04). The authors caution that the effect of introducing a standardized protocol is difficult to separate from its individual components. Consistent checklist use may be important both for adopting and sustaining shunt infection prevention.

document_sections.heading: Study Strengths and Limitations
document_sections.content: The authors identify prospective data collection as a strength because it permitted assessment of timing between protocol changes and infection rates. They also cite the large series of n = 621 procedures, described as the largest reported adult shunt infection prevention series to date. IPC jointly implemented the protocol, independently monitored procedures for infection, and met routinely with neurosurgery about infections and adherence. Selection bias was considered limited because most eligible adult VP shunt insertions and revisions at the center were included. As FMC is the only shunt surgery center in southern Alberta, the authors considered the population diverse and representative of regional adults with hydrocephalus. They describe CASIPP’s measures as straightforward, achievable, and unambiguous; because the protocol requires neither intrathecal antibiotics nor AICs, they believe it could be transferred readily and economically to other centers. Limitations include its single-center setting and operations by only one surgeon with particular shunt expertise. The nonrandomized design prevented control of unknown confounding. Other changes during the study, including neuronavigation for proximal catheter insertion and laparoscopic placement of the distal catheter, were not accounted for and might have affected results. The authors consider those techniques important for reducing overall shunt failure but unlikely to lower surgical infection risk. For patients treated before CASIPP, the specific preventive steps used, including the frequency of double gloving or chlorhexidine use, were uncertain, although baseline infection-rate data were available. The small number of infections limited precise estimation of protocol effects and the ability to apply complex analyses controlling for possible within-patient correlation; each of the 11 infections occurred in a different patient.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that a standardized prevention protocol can significantly reduce adult shunt infections. They consider the addition of preoperative 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol likely to have contributed substantially, while also attributing importance to continued monitoring and protocol adjustment. They believe CASIPP can be readily adopted elsewhere and call for larger multicenter studies to verify its effectiveness.
